# How to use this guide

Cell and Molecular Biology is **one of the semester-8 electives** of the PCI B.Pharm course. It has no practical; the whole subject is the 75-mark theory paper. The subject is descriptive: there are almost no calculations, and marks come from clear, well-labelled diagrams, step-by-step mechanisms and comparison tables. Study one unit a day: read the notes, draw each diagram once from memory (double helix, replication fork, tRNA cloverleaf, lac operon, cell cycle, apoptosis pathways, G protein cycle, kinase cascade), then answer the question bank. Each unit has very short (2-mark), short answer (5-mark) and long essay (10-mark) questions, rated by how often that kind of question appears in PCI-syllabus papers.

The five units follow the five units of the PCI syllabus. A few textbook topics that the syllabus words point to but do not name are placed where they fit best: DNA replication, repair and mutation are under "DNA functioning" in Unit 2; gene regulation (lac and trp operons) is under "positive control of protein synthesis" in Unit 3; and apoptosis is with the cell cycle checkpoints in Unit 4.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ questions | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; prepare the full answer with a labelled diagram and a table.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from common patterns and syllabus weight, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Cells and chemical foundations | Fluid mosaic model, membrane transport, prokaryotic vs eukaryotic cells, history milestones, properties of cells, bonds and types of biochemical reactions |
| 2 DNA and RNA | Watson–Crick model, semiconservative replication and its enzymes, types of RNA, transcription in prokaryotes and eukaryotes, mRNA processing, genetic code, translation steps |
| 3 Proteins and gene control | Amino acid classification, four levels of protein structure, protein targeting and post-translational modification, lac operon with positive control, significance of protein synthesis |
| 4 Genetics and cell cycle | Mendel's laws, recombinant DNA and transgenic animals, PCR, phases of the cell cycle, mitosis vs meiosis, cyclins/CDKs and checkpoints, apoptosis |
| 5 Cell signalling | Types of signalling, receptor families, GPCR–cAMP and IP3–DAG pathways, RTK–Ras–MAPK, misregulation in cancer, protein kinases and their inhibitors |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. Start each answer with a one-line definition, then a labelled diagram, then the steps in numbered order. Mechanism questions (replication, transcription, translation, signalling) are marked step by step.
2. Use comparison tables with at least six points for the classic "differentiate" questions: prokaryote vs eukaryote, DNA vs RNA, mitosis vs meiosis, apoptosis vs necrosis, prokaryotic vs eukaryotic transcription or translation, negative vs positive control.
3. Name the enzyme or factor at every step (helicase, primase, pol III, ligase; sigma factor; EF-Tu, EF-G; caspase-9, caspase-3). Missing names cost the most marks in this paper.
4. Always end with pharmaceutical relevance: antibiotics acting on bacterial replication, transcription and ribosomes; anticancer drugs acting on the cell cycle; kinase inhibitors; recombinant medicines. This links the elective to your degree and examiners reward it.
5. Learn the few exact facts that MCQs test: 3.4 nm pitch and about 10 bp per turn of B-DNA; A=T two and G≡C three hydrogen bonds; −10 TATAAT and −35 TTGACA; start AUG and stops UAA, UAG, UGA; 70S = 50S + 30S, 80S = 60S + 40S; α-helix 3.6 residues per turn; Na+/K+-ATPase 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in; PCR temperatures.
6. Spell the history correctly with the right decade (Hooke 1665, Watson and Crick 1953, Meselson–Stahl 1958, Jacob–Monod 1961, Singer–Nicolson 1972). If you are not sure of a year, write the scientist and the finding without the date.
7. In signalling answers, draw the pathway as a chain of arrows from receptor to response and show how it is switched off; this alone earns a large part of the marks.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you only have an hour, learn these five topics with full diagrams: **DNA replication (enzymes and fork)**, **transcription and mRNA processing**, **translation with the genetic code**, **lac operon (negative and positive control)**, and **GPCR second-messenger pathways**. Add **cell cycle checkpoints with apoptosis** if you have time. Together they cover most 10-mark questions.

**Unit 1 — Cells and chemical foundations**

- Cell theory: Schleiden and Schwann (1838–39); Virchow — every cell from a cell (1855).
- Fluid mosaic model (Singer–Nicolson 1972): phospholipid bilayer + integral/peripheral proteins + cholesterol + glycocalyx; about 7–10 nm.
- Transport: simple diffusion, facilitated (channels, GLUT), primary active (Na+/K+-ATPase, 3 out/2 in), secondary active (SGLT), endo/exocytosis.
- Prokaryote: no nucleus, circular DNA, 70S, peptidoglycan, binary fission. Eukaryote: nucleus, histones, 80S, organelles, mitosis.
- Bonds: covalent; weak = hydrogen, ionic, van der Waals, hydrophobic. Reactions: redox, group transfer, hydrolysis, condensation, isomerisation, C–C bond making/breaking.
- ΔG < 0 exergonic; ATP hydrolysis about −30.5 kJ/mol; enzymes lower activation energy only.

**Unit 2 — DNA and RNA**

| Item | Fact |
| --- | --- |
| B-DNA | Right-handed, antiparallel, about 10 bp/turn, 3.4 nm pitch, 2 nm wide |
| Base pairs | A=T (2 H-bonds), G≡C (3 H-bonds); Chargaff A = T, G = C |
| Replication | Semiconservative (Meselson–Stahl); helicase, SSB, gyrase, primase, pol III, pol I, ligase |
| Strands | Leading continuous; lagging as Okazaki fragments |
| Telomerase | RNA-containing reverse transcriptase; TTAGGG repeats |
| Cell RNA | rRNA about 80%, tRNA 15%, mRNA 5% |
| Ribosomes | 70S = 50S (23S, 5S) + 30S (16S); 80S = 60S (28S, 5.8S, 5S) + 40S (18S) |
| Bacterial promoter | −10 TATAAT (Pribnow), −35 TTGACA; σ factor |
| Eukaryotic RNA pols | I = rRNA; II = mRNA (α-amanitin sensitive); III = tRNA, 5S |
| mRNA processing | 5′ cap, splicing (GU…AG), poly-A tail |
| Code | 64 codons; AUG start; UAA, UAG, UGA stop; degenerate; wobble |
| Translation | Shine–Dalgarno; A, P, E sites; EF-Tu, peptidyl transferase (23S rRNA), EF-G; RF1/RF2 |

**Unit 3 — Proteins and gene control**

- 20 amino acids, L-form; glycine non-chiral; 9 essential in adults (His, Ile, Leu, Lys, Met, Phe, Thr, Trp, Val).
- Structure: primary (sequence) → secondary (α-helix 3.6/turn, β-sheet) → tertiary → quaternary (haemoglobin α2β2).
- Targeting: signal peptide + SRP → ER → Golgi; M6P → lysosome; NLS → nucleus. Degradation: ubiquitin → 26S proteasome.
- lac operon: lacZ, lacY, lacA; repressor (lacI) removed by allolactose; CAP–cAMP activates when glucose is low (positive control). trp operon: repressible, tryptophan = corepressor, attenuation.

**Unit 4 — Genetics and cell cycle**

- Mendel: 3:1 and 9:3:3:1. Autosomal recessive: sickle cell, CF, PKU. X-linked: haemophilia, G6PD deficiency.
- rDNA: restriction enzyme (EcoRI G^AATTC) → ligase → plasmid → transformation → selection.
- PCR: 94–95 °C / 50–65 °C / 72 °C, Taq. Southern DNA, Northern RNA, Western protein.
- Cycle: G1 → S → G2 → M; G0 resting. CDK4/6–D, CDK2–E, CDK1–B (MPF). Rb–E2F; p53 → p21.
- Checkpoints: G1/S, intra-S, G2/M, spindle assembly (Mad2, APC/C).
- Apoptosis: intrinsic (Bax/Bak → cytochrome c → Apaf-1 → caspase-9) and extrinsic (Fas/TNF → FADD → caspase-8) → caspase-3; DNA ladder; no inflammation.

**Unit 5 — Cell signalling**

| Pathway | Sequence |
| --- | --- |
| Gs | Receptor → Gs → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA → CREB |
| Gq | Receptor → Gq → PLC-β → IP3 (Ca2+) + DAG (PKC) |
| NO | NO → soluble guanylyl cyclase → cGMP → PKG; PDE5 breaks cGMP |
| RTK | Dimerise → autophosphorylate → Grb2–SOS → Ras → Raf → MEK → ERK |
| Insulin | IRS → PI3K → PIP3 → Akt → GLUT4 |
| Cytokine | Receptor → JAK → STAT → nucleus |

- Receptor families: ion channel (ms), GPCR (s), enzyme-linked (min–h), nuclear (h–days).
- Off switches: GTPase, PDE, phosphatases, GRK + β-arrestin.
- Misregulation: mutant Ras, BCR-ABL (imatinib), HER2, EGFR, BRAF V600E; cholera toxin (Gs on), pertussis toxin (Gi off).
- Kinases: ATP γ-phosphate → Ser/Thr/Tyr; ATP cleft is the drug site ("-tinib" drugs).

questions.answer:
1. Definition: the plasma membrane is the 7–10 nm boundary of the cell; Singer and Nicolson (1972) described it as a fluid lipid bilayer with proteins floating in it like a mosaic.
2. Diagram: bilayer with polar heads outside and fatty acid tails inside; integral protein crossing it; peripheral protein on the surface; glycoprotein and glycolipid sugars facing outward.
3. Lipids: phospholipids (amphipathic; PC, PE, PS, sphingomyelin) form the barrier; cholesterol controls fluidity; glycolipids act in recognition.
4. Proteins: integral (channels, carriers, receptors), peripheral (enzymes, cytoskeleton links), lipid-anchored (Ras).
5. Carbohydrates: glycocalyx on the outer face — recognition, adhesion.
6. Properties: fluidity (lateral movement; increased by unsaturated short chains and heat, buffered by cholesterol) and asymmetry (PS on inner face; outer exposure signals apoptosis).
7. Functions: selective barrier, transport, receptors for signals, cell recognition and junctions, anchoring cytoskeleton, keeping ion gradients and membrane potential.
8. Transport: simple diffusion (O2, CO2, lipid-soluble drugs); facilitated diffusion by channels (K+ channels, aquaporins) and carriers (GLUT, saturable); primary active transport (Na+/K+-ATPase, 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP); secondary active transport (Na+–glucose symport, Na+/Ca2+ exchange); endocytosis (phagocytosis, pinocytosis, receptor-mediated LDL uptake) and exocytosis.
9. Pharmaceutical note: most drugs cross by passive diffusion of the un-ionised form; P-glycoprotein efflux causes drug resistance.
questions.question: Describe the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane. Add a note on the functions of the membrane and the mechanisms of transport across it.

questions.answer:
1. Prokaryotes (bacteria, archaea) lack a true nucleus; eukaryotes (protozoa, fungi, plants, animals) have one.
2. Comparison table: size 1–10 µm vs 10–100 µm; nucleoid vs nucleus with double envelope; circular DNA with few histones vs linear chromosomes on histones; 70S vs 80S ribosomes; no membrane organelles vs mitochondria, ER, Golgi, lysosomes; peptidoglycan wall vs none (animals) or cellulose/chitin; binary fission vs mitosis/meiosis; coupled vs separate transcription and translation; introns rare vs common; simple flagella vs 9+2 flagella.
3. Nucleus: double membrane with pores, nucleolus makes rRNA; stores DNA, site of replication and transcription.
4. Rough ER: ribosome-studded; makes secretory and membrane proteins. Smooth ER: lipid synthesis, cytochrome P450 drug metabolism, Ca2+ store.
5. Golgi: cis to trans stacks; glycosylation, sorting, packaging into vesicles.
6. Lysosomes: acid hydrolases at about pH 5; digestion and autophagy.
7. Mitochondria: double membrane, cristae, own DNA and ribosomes; ATP by oxidative phosphorylation; release cytochrome c in apoptosis.
8. Peroxisomes: catalase, fatty acid oxidation. Ribosomes: protein synthesis. Cytoskeleton: microfilaments (7 nm), intermediate filaments (10 nm), microtubules (25 nm). Centrosome: spindle organisation.
9. Relevance: selective toxicity of antibiotics — penicillins (cell wall), tetracyclines and aminoglycosides (30S), macrolides and chloramphenicol (50S), fluoroquinolones (DNA gyrase).
questions.question: Differentiate prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. Describe the structure and functions of the main eukaryotic organelles.

questions.answer:
1. Hooke (1665) named cells in cork; Leeuwenhoek (1670s) saw living cells; Brown (1831) the nucleus.
2. Schleiden and Schwann (1838–39) — cell theory; Virchow (1855) — every cell from a cell.
3. Mendel (1866) — laws of inheritance; Miescher (1869) — nuclein.
4. Griffith (1928) transformation; Avery, MacLeod and McCarty (1944) — DNA is the transforming principle; Hershey and Chase (1952) confirmed it.
5. Chargaff's base ratios; Watson and Crick (1953) — double helix; Meselson and Stahl (1958) — semiconservative replication.
6. Crick (1958) — central dogma; Jacob and Monod (1961) — operon; Nirenberg and Khorana — genetic code; Temin and Baltimore (1970) — reverse transcriptase.
7. Singer–Nicolson (1972) membrane model; Cohen–Boyer (1973) recombinant DNA; Sanger (1977) sequencing; Mullis (1983) PCR; Human Genome Project (2003).
8. Cell theory: all organisms are made of cells; cell is the unit of structure and function; cells come only from cells; plus DNA as hereditary material.
9. Central dogma: DNA → DNA (replication), DNA → RNA (transcription), RNA → protein (translation); exceptions reverse transcription and RNA replication.
10. Applications: drug target discovery, recombinant proteins (insulin, growth hormone, erythropoietin), monoclonal antibodies, vaccines, PCR diagnosis, gene therapy, pharmacogenomics, understanding cancer and toxicity.
questions.question: Trace the history of cell and molecular biology. Explain the cell theory and the central dogma, and list the applications of the subject in pharmacy.

questions.answer:
1. Highly complex and organised.
2. Possess a genetic program (DNA) and the means to use it.
3. Reproduce by division.
4. Acquire and use energy (ATP).
5. Carry out chemical reactions (metabolism) catalysed by enzymes.
6. Perform mechanical activities (transport, contraction, cilia, chromosome movement).
7. Respond to stimuli through receptors.
8. Self-regulate (homeostasis, repair).
9. Evolve. Cells are small (bacteria about 1–5 µm, animal cells 10–30 µm) because a high surface-to-volume ratio allows fast exchange.
questions.question: List the general properties of living cells.

questions.answer:
1. Active transport moves solutes against their concentration gradient and needs energy.
2. Primary active transport uses ATP directly: Na+/K+-ATPase pumps 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP; also Ca2+-ATPase, H+/K+-ATPase of gastric parietal cells (target of proton pump inhibitors).
3. Secondary active transport uses the energy stored in an ion gradient made by a primary pump.
4. Symport: Na+ and glucose move in together (SGLT in gut and kidney).
5. Antiport: Na+ in, Ca2+ out (Na+/Ca2+ exchanger in heart muscle).
6. Both are carrier-mediated, saturable and specific, unlike simple diffusion.
questions.question: Explain primary and secondary active transport with examples.

questions.answer:
1. Covalent bonds: strong, shared electrons; form backbones — peptide, phosphodiester, glycosidic bonds.
2. Ionic bonds: between opposite charges; salt bridges in proteins; weak in water.
3. Hydrogen bonds: between H on N or O and another N or O; base pairing in DNA, α-helix and β-sheet.
4. Van der Waals forces: weak, short-range attractions; close packing, drug–receptor fit.
5. Hydrophobic interactions: non-polar groups cluster away from water; drive membrane formation and protein folding.
6. Many weak bonds together give stable but reversible structures — DNA strands can separate, drugs can bind and leave.
questions.question: Describe the types of chemical bonds and interactions important in biological molecules.

questions.answer:
1. Oxidation–reduction: electron transfer with NAD+/FAD carriers; glucose oxidation to CO2.
2. Group transfer: phosphate from ATP to glucose by hexokinase.
3. Hydrolysis: breaking bonds with water; protein digestion by proteases.
4. Condensation (dehydration): joining with loss of water; peptide bond formation.
5. Isomerisation: glucose 6-phosphate ⇌ fructose 6-phosphate.
6. Making or breaking C–C bonds: aldolase splitting fructose 1,6-bisphosphate.
7. Elimination/addition across double bonds: dehydratases.
8. Energetics: exergonic (ΔG < 0) reactions proceed alone; endergonic ones are coupled to ATP hydrolysis (about −30.5 kJ/mol); enzymes lower activation energy.

questions.answer:
1. Replication is semiconservative (Meselson–Stahl, ¹⁵N/¹⁴N density experiment) and bidirectional from an origin (oriC).
2. Initiation: DnaA binds oriC; helicase (DnaB) unwinds; SSB proteins hold strands apart; DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) removes supercoils.
3. Priming: primase makes short RNA primers.
4. Elongation: DNA polymerase III adds dNTPs to the 3′-OH, 5′→3′, with 3′→5′ proofreading; sliding clamp gives processivity.
5. Leading strand made continuously; lagging strand discontinuously as Okazaki fragments (1000–2000 nt).
6. DNA polymerase I removes primers and fills gaps; DNA ligase seals nicks.
7. Termination at ter sites where forks meet.
8. Diagram: fork with helicase, SSB, primase, pol III on both strands, Okazaki fragments, ligase.
9. Eukaryotic differences: many origins; polymerases α (with primase), δ (lagging), ε (leading); nucleosome reassembly; once per cycle in S phase; telomerase solves the end-replication problem by adding TTAGGG repeats.
10. Fidelity: about one error per 10^9–10^10 bases; drugs: fluoroquinolones inhibit gyrase; antimetabolites stop DNA synthesis.
questions.question: Describe the mechanism of DNA replication in prokaryotes with a labelled diagram of the replication fork. Mention how eukaryotic replication differs.

questions.answer:
1. Transcription = RNA synthesis on a DNA template by RNA polymerase; template strand read 3′→5′; RNA grows 5′→3′; no primer.
2. Prokaryotic RNA polymerase: core α2ββ′ω + σ factor = holoenzyme; σ recognises the promoter (−35 TTGACA, −10 TATAAT Pribnow box).
3. Initiation: closed then open complex, first phosphodiester bond.
4. Elongation: σ released; core moves with a transcription bubble.
5. Termination: rho-independent (GC-rich hairpin followed by U's) or rho-dependent (rho helicase).
6. Bacterial mRNA is polycistronic and translated as it forms.
7. Eukaryotes: RNA pol I (28S, 18S, 5.8S rRNA), II (mRNA; α-amanitin sensitive), III (tRNA, 5S rRNA); TATA box bound by TBP in TFIID; general transcription factors; TFIIH phosphorylates the polymerase tail; enhancers and activators.
8. Processing: 5′ 7-methylguanosine cap (protection, ribosome binding); splicing of introns (GU…AG) by spliceosome snRNPs, alternative splicing; cleavage after AAUAAA and poly-A tail; export through nuclear pores.
9. Drugs: rifampicin (bacterial RNA polymerase β subunit), actinomycin D (intercalates).
questions.question: Explain the process of transcription in prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Describe the post-transcriptional processing of eukaryotic mRNA.

questions.answer:
1. Charging: aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase links amino acid to tRNA using ATP; ensures accuracy.
2. Ribosome sites: A (aminoacyl), P (peptidyl), E (exit); 70S = 50S + 30S.
3. Initiation: 30S binds mRNA at the Shine–Dalgarno sequence (pairs with 16S rRNA); fMet-tRNA pairs with AUG in the P site; IF1, IF2-GTP, IF3; 50S joins.
4. Elongation: EF-Tu-GTP delivers aa-tRNA to A site; peptidyl transferase (23S rRNA ribozyme) forms the peptide bond; EF-G-GTP translocates the ribosome by one codon; empty tRNA leaves via E site.
5. Termination: stop codon in A site; RF1 (UAA, UAG), RF2 (UAA, UGA), RF3; polypeptide released; subunits separate. Polysomes form; about 4 high-energy bonds per peptide bond.
6. Genetic code: triplet; 64 codons (61 sense, 3 stop); AUG start; degenerate; unambiguous; non-overlapping, comma-less; nearly universal (mitochondrial UGA = Trp); wobble at third base.
7. Antibiotics: aminoglycosides (30S, misreading), tetracyclines (30S, block A site), chloramphenicol (50S, peptidyl transferase), macrolides (50S, exit tunnel/translocation), linezolid (blocks initiation complex), puromycin (premature termination).
questions.question: Describe the steps of protein synthesis (translation) in prokaryotes. Write the properties of the genetic code and name antibiotics acting on bacterial ribosomes.

questions.answer:
1. Two polynucleotide strands form a right-handed double helix around a common axis.
2. Strands are antiparallel (5′→3′ and 3′→5′).
3. Sugar–phosphate backbone outside; bases stacked inside.
4. Complementary pairing: A=T (2 hydrogen bonds), G≡C (3 hydrogen bonds); explains Chargaff's rules.
5. Dimensions: diameter 2 nm, about 10 bp and 3.4 nm per turn, 0.34 nm between base pairs.
6. Major and minor grooves for protein and drug binding.
7. Complementarity explains how DNA is copied (each strand is a template). Other forms: A-DNA (right-handed, 11 bp) and Z-DNA (left-handed, 12 bp).
questions.question: Describe the Watson–Crick model of DNA.

questions.answer:
1. rRNA (about 80%): forms ribosomes; 23S/28S rRNA catalyses peptide bonds. Prokaryotes 23S, 5S, 16S; eukaryotes 28S, 5.8S, 5S, 18S.
2. tRNA (about 15%): 75–90 nucleotides; carries amino acids; anticodon reads codon.
3. mRNA (about 5%): carries the code; eukaryotic mRNA has 5′ cap and poly-A tail.
4. snRNA: splicing; snoRNA: rRNA modification; miRNA and siRNA: gene silencing; lncRNA: chromatin regulation; ribozymes: catalysis.
5. Cloverleaf: acceptor stem with 3′ CCA end (amino acid attached), D arm, anticodon arm with anticodon loop, variable loop, TψC arm; folds to an L-shape in 3D.
questions.question: Describe the types of RNA and their functions. Draw the cloverleaf structure of tRNA.

questions.answer:
1. Point mutations: transitions (purine↔purine) and transversions (purine↔pyrimidine).
2. Effects: silent, missense (sickle cell Glu→Val), nonsense (premature stop), frameshift (insertion/deletion).
3. Causes: replication errors, deamination, UV (thymine dimers), radiation, alkylating agents, intercalators.
4. Repair: direct reversal (photolyase, methyltransferase); base excision (glycosylase); nucleotide excision (bulky lesions; defect = xeroderma pigmentosum); mismatch repair (defect = Lynch syndrome); double-strand break repair by homologous recombination (BRCA1/2) and non-homologous end joining.
5. Anticancer drugs exploit DNA damage faster than repair.
questions.question: Explain the types of mutation and the DNA repair mechanisms.

questions.answer:
1. Sugar: deoxyribose vs ribose.
2. Bases: T in DNA, U in RNA.
3. Strands: usually double vs usually single.
4. Stability: DNA stable; RNA hydrolysed easily in alkali due to 2′-OH.
5. Location: DNA in nucleus (and mitochondria); RNA made in nucleus, works mostly in cytoplasm.
6. Function: long-term information store vs carrying, decoding, catalysing and regulating.
7. Amount: DNA constant per cell; RNA varies with activity.
8. Synthesis: DNA polymerase vs RNA polymerase; types: one DNA vs many RNAs (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA, small RNAs).
questions.question: Differentiate between DNA and RNA.

questions.answer: Short DNA pieces (about 1000–2000 nucleotides in bacteria, 100–200 in eukaryotes) made discontinuously on the lagging strand during replication, each started from an RNA primer and later joined by DNA ligase.
questions.question: What are Okazaki fragments?

questions.answer: Start codon: AUG (methionine; N-formylmethionine in bacteria). Stop codons: UAA, UAG and UGA.
questions.question: Name the stop codons and the start codon.

questions.answer:
1. Operon (Jacob and Monod, 1961): genes under one promoter and operator transcribed as one mRNA; lac operon is inducible (catabolic).
2. Parts: regulator gene lacI (repressor), CAP binding site, promoter, operator, structural genes lacZ (β-galactosidase), lacY (permease), lacA (transacetylase).
3. Diagram of the operon layout.
4. Negative control: in the absence of lactose the repressor binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase.
5. Induction: lactose → allolactose (inducer) binds the repressor and changes its shape; repressor leaves the operator. IPTG is a synthetic inducer.
6. Positive control: low glucose → cAMP rises → cAMP binds CAP (CRP) → CAP–cAMP binds next to the promoter, bends DNA and recruits RNA polymerase → strong transcription.
7. Catabolite repression: high glucose → low cAMP → no CAP binding → operon stays low even with lactose; glucose is used first.
8. Four-condition table (glucose/lactose) showing the operon is fully on only with lactose present and glucose absent.
9. Significance: economy of protein synthesis; model for gene regulation; lac promoter with IPTG used to express recombinant proteins in E. coli.
questions.question: Describe the structure of the lac operon. Explain its negative and positive control and the significance of catabolite repression.

questions.answer:
1. Proteins: polymers of amino acids linked by peptide bonds, folded into a specific 3D shape that decides function.
2. Amino acid structure: α-carbon with NH2, COOH, H and R group; L-form; glycine achiral; zwitterion; isoelectric point.
3. Classification by R group: non-polar aliphatic (Gly, Ala, Val, Leu, Ile, Met, Pro); aromatic (Phe, Tyr, Trp); polar uncharged (Ser, Thr, Cys, Asn, Gln); basic (Lys, Arg, His); acidic (Asp, Glu). Nutritional: 9 essential in adults.
4. Peptide bond: planar, partial double bond, trans.
5. Primary structure: sequence; peptide bonds and disulphide bonds; sickle cell example.
6. Secondary: α-helix (right-handed, 3.6 residues per turn, 0.54 nm pitch, H-bond n to n+4) and β-sheet (parallel/antiparallel); backbone hydrogen bonds.
7. Tertiary: 3D folding of one chain; hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, van der Waals, disulphide bridges; domains.
8. Quaternary: subunit arrangement; haemoglobin α2β2, antibodies.
9. Denaturation, Anfinsen's experiment and chaperones; pharmaceutical relevance for protein drug stability.
questions.question: Define proteins. Classify amino acids and describe the four levels of protein structure with the bonds involved.

questions.answer:
1. Proteins carry sorting signals in their sequence.
2. Cytosolic proteins: no signal, made on free ribosomes.
3. Secretory pathway: N-terminal signal peptide → SRP halts translation → SRP receptor on ER → translocon → signal peptidase; folding, N-glycosylation, disulphide bonds in ER → vesicles → Golgi (cis to trans; O-glycosylation, sorting) → secretion, membrane or lysosome.
4. Other signals: KDEL (ER retention), mannose-6-phosphate (lysosome; I-cell disease), nuclear localisation signal (importins), mitochondrial presequence (TOM/TIM), SKL (peroxisome).
5. Post-translational modifications: proteolytic cleavage (proinsulin → insulin, zymogens), phosphorylation, glycosylation, disulphide bonds, acetylation/methylation, prenylation (Ras), hydroxylation (collagen, vitamin C), γ-carboxylation (clotting factors, vitamin K, warfarin), ubiquitination.
6. Degradation: ubiquitin (E1, E2, E3) marks proteins for the 26S proteasome (bortezomib inhibits it); lysosomal pathway and autophagy.
7. Regular features of metabolic pathways: committed step, feedback inhibition, separate enzymes for opposing pathways, control by amount, allostery and phosphorylation.
questions.question: Describe the regular pathways followed by proteins after synthesis: targeting, post-translational modification and degradation.

questions.answer:
1. Expression of genetic information — genes act through proteins.
2. Growth, repair and replacement of tissues.
3. Production of enzymes, hormones, antibodies, receptors and transporters.
4. Adaptation by induction of enzymes (lac operon; enzyme induction by rifampicin and phenobarbital).
5. Selective target for antibiotics because 70S and 80S ribosomes differ.
6. Errors cause disease (sickle cell, cystic fibrosis); uncontrolled synthesis contributes to cancer.
7. Basis of biotechnology — recombinant insulin, interferons, growth hormone, erythropoietin, monoclonal antibodies, vaccine antigens.
questions.question: Explain the significance of protein synthesis.

questions.answer:
1. Negative control: a repressor protein binding DNA switches transcription off; inducer or corepressor changes repressor activity.
2. Positive control: an activator protein binding DNA switches transcription on or increases it.
3. Inducible negative control: lac repressor removed by allolactose.
4. Repressible negative control: trp repressor activated by tryptophan (corepressor).
5. Positive control: CAP–cAMP activates the lac operon when glucose is low; ara operon AraC.
6. In eukaryotes positive control dominates: activators on enhancers recruit co-activators; steroid receptors are hormone-activated transcription factors.
7. Table comparing regulator, effect of binding, and examples.
questions.question: Differentiate negative and positive control of gene expression with examples.

questions.answer:
1. Folding is driven mainly by burying hydrophobic side chains; the sequence contains the folding information (Anfinsen's ribonuclease experiment).
2. Denaturation: loss of native 3D shape and activity without breaking peptide bonds; caused by heat, extreme pH, urea, guanidine, detergents, solvents, heavy metals.
3. Renaturation is possible for some small proteins.
4. Chaperones: Hsp70 binds exposed hydrophobic regions; chaperonins (Hsp60, GroEL–GroES) provide a folding chamber; protein disulphide isomerase and prolyl isomerase speed slow steps.
5. Misfolding diseases: Alzheimer's (β-amyloid), Parkinson's (α-synuclein), prion diseases.
6. Pharmacy: protein drugs need cold chain and stabilisers.
questions.question: Write a note on protein folding, denaturation and molecular chaperones.

questions.answer:
1. The trp operon has five structural genes (trpE, D, C, B, A) for tryptophan synthesis; it is a repressible (anabolic) operon.
2. The repressor is made inactive; tryptophan (corepressor) binds and activates it.
3. Active repressor binds the operator and stops transcription when tryptophan is plentiful.
4. Attenuation: a leader sequence codes a short peptide with two Trp codons; when charged Trp-tRNA is abundant the ribosome moves fast and a terminator hairpin forms, ending transcription early; when Trp is scarce the ribosome stalls and an antiterminator forms, so transcription continues.
5. Gives fine control in addition to repression.
questions.question: Describe the trp operon and attenuation.

questions.answer: An amino acid that the body cannot make in enough amount and must take from the diet; for example leucine, lysine, methionine, tryptophan (others: histidine, isoleucine, phenylalanine, threonine, valine).
questions.question: What is an essential amino acid? Name any four.

questions.answer: It binds the signal peptide of a protein as it emerges from the ribosome, pauses translation and brings the ribosome to the SRP receptor on the ER so the protein enters the secretory pathway.
questions.question: What is the role of the signal recognition particle?

questions.answer:
1. Cell cycle: G1 (growth), S (DNA replication), G2 (preparation), M (mitosis and cytokinesis); G0 = resting state; typical 24 h cycle (G1 about 11 h, S 8 h, G2 4 h, M 1 h).
2. Diagram of the cycle with checkpoints marked.
3. CDKs are kinases active only with cyclins whose levels rise and fall: CDK4/6–cyclin D (G1), CDK2–cyclin E (G1/S), CDK2–cyclin A (S), CDK1–cyclin B = MPF (G2/M).
4. Cyclins are destroyed by ubiquitin–proteasome (APC/C for mitotic cyclins).
5. CDK inhibitors: p21, p27 (Cip/Kip), p16 (INK4).
6. Rb–E2F: phosphorylation of Rb frees E2F → S-phase genes; restriction point commits the cell.
7. Checkpoints: G1/S (size, nutrients, signals, DNA damage); intra-S (ATR, Chk1); G2/M (complete and correct replication; ATM/ATR, Chk1/Chk2); spindle assembly (all kinetochores attached; Mad2, APC/C, securin, separase, cohesin).
8. p53: activated by ATM/ATR after DNA damage → p21 (arrest), repair genes, or apoptosis (Bax, Puma).
9. Cancer: oncogenes (Ras, Myc) and loss of tumour suppressors (p53, Rb).
10. Drugs: S-phase antimetabolites, M-phase vinca alkaloids and taxanes, CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib.
questions.question: Describe the phases of the cell cycle. Explain the role of cyclins, CDKs and the checkpoints that control it.

questions.answer:
1. Mitosis: equational division of somatic cells.
2. Prophase: chromatin condenses, sister chromatids visible, nucleolus disappears, spindle forms. Prometaphase: envelope breaks, kinetochores attach. Metaphase: chromosomes at equatorial plate. Anaphase: cohesin cleaved, chromatids move to poles. Telophase: nuclei re-form. Cytokinesis: actin–myosin ring (animal), cell plate (plant). Result: 2 identical diploid cells.
3. Meiosis I: prophase I — leptotene, zygotene (synapsis), pachytene (crossing over), diplotene (chiasmata), diakinesis; metaphase I — bivalents at the plate; anaphase I — homologues separate; telophase I — two haploid cells.
4. Meiosis II: like mitosis, no prior replication; sister chromatids separate. Result: 4 haploid, genetically different cells.
5. Differences: somatic vs germ cells; one vs two divisions; 2 vs 4 cells; 2n→2n vs 2n→n; no pairing vs synapsis; no crossing over vs crossing over; identical vs varied products; growth/repair vs gamete formation.
6. Significance: meiosis gives variation; errors (non-disjunction) cause Down syndrome, Turner and Klinefelter syndromes.
questions.question: Describe mitosis and meiosis with diagrams and give their differences.

questions.answer:
1. Tools: restriction endonucleases (EcoRI G^AATTC, sticky or blunt ends), DNA ligase, vectors (plasmids with ori, selectable marker and cloning site; phage λ; cosmids; BAC, YAC; viral vectors), hosts (E. coli, yeast, CHO cells), reverse transcriptase for cDNA.
2. Steps: isolate gene → cut gene and vector → ligate → transform host (CaCl2/heat shock, electroporation) → select (antibiotic resistance, blue–white screening) → grow and express → purify.
3. Transgenic animals: carry a foreign gene in all cells; made by pronuclear microinjection, embryonic stem cells (knockout mice), retroviral vectors, nuclear transfer. Plants by Agrobacterium Ti plasmid or gene gun.
4. Applications: disease models, pharming (antithrombin in goat milk), recombinant insulin, growth hormone, hepatitis B vaccine, erythropoietin, monoclonal antibodies, Bt cotton, gene therapy.
5. Genomic analysis: PCR (94–95 °C, 50–65 °C, 72 °C, Taq; RT-PCR, real-time PCR); gel electrophoresis; Southern, Northern, Western blots; Sanger and next-generation sequencing; microarrays/RNA-seq; proteomics; DNA fingerprinting; CRISPR–Cas9 editing.
6. Concerns: biosafety, ethics; in India the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee approves release of GE organisms.
questions.question: Explain recombinant DNA technology and the production of transgenic animals. Add a note on methods of genomic analysis and their applications.

questions.answer:
1. Apoptosis: programmed, ATP-dependent; single cells; cell shrinks; membrane intact with blebs and apoptotic bodies; DNA ladder (about 180–200 bp); no inflammation. Necrosis: injury-driven; groups of cells; swelling; membrane rupture; random DNA breakdown; inflammation.
2. Intrinsic pathway: DNA damage/stress → BH3-only proteins → Bax/Bak pores → cytochrome c release → Apaf-1 apoptosome → caspase-9 → caspase-3/7.
3. Extrinsic pathway: FasL/TNF/TRAIL → death receptor → FADD → caspase-8 → caspase-3; Bid → tBid links pathways.
4. Bcl-2 and Bcl-xL block apoptosis; IAPs inhibit caspases.
5. Detection: DNA ladder, TUNEL, annexin V, caspase assays.
questions.question: Differentiate apoptosis and necrosis and outline the pathways of apoptosis.

questions.answer:
1. Law of dominance: in a cross of pure contrasting forms only the dominant trait shows in F1.
2. Law of segregation: allele pairs separate at gamete formation; Tt × Tt gives 3:1 phenotype and 1:2:1 genotype ratio (Punnett square).
3. Law of independent assortment: genes on different chromosomes sort independently; dihybrid F2 ratio 9:3:3:1.
4. Basis: behaviour of chromosomes in meiosis (chromosome theory).
5. Exceptions: linkage (Morgan), incomplete dominance, co-dominance (AB blood group), multiple alleles, polygenic traits, epistasis.
questions.question: State and explain Mendel's laws of inheritance.

questions.answer:
1. Flow cytometry with a DNA dye such as propidium iodide: G1 cells 2n, G2/M cells 4n, S-phase intermediate; sub-G1 peak = apoptotic cells.
2. S-phase labelling with ³H-thymidine or BrdU (detected by antibody).
3. Mitotic index by microscopy.
4. Synchronisation: thymidine block (G1/S), nocodazole or colchicine (mitosis), then release.
5. Western blotting of cyclins and phosphorylated proteins.
6. Time-lapse microscopy of live cells.
7. Uses: studying anticancer drugs and how they arrest cells.
questions.question: Describe the methods used for cell cycle analysis.

questions.answer:
1. p53 is a tumour-suppressor transcription factor kept at low level by MDM2-mediated degradation.
2. DNA damage activates ATM/ATR kinases, which phosphorylate and stabilise p53.
3. p53 switches on p21, which inhibits CDKs and arrests the cell in G1 (and G2) for repair.
4. It activates DNA-repair genes.
5. If damage is too great it switches on pro-apoptotic genes (Bax, Puma, Noxa) → apoptosis.
6. Mutated in about half of human cancers; loss lets damaged cells divide; many anticancer drugs need functional p53 for full effect.
questions.question: Explain the role of p53 as the guardian of the genome.

questions.answer: An animal that carries a foreign gene (transgene) deliberately inserted into its genome in all its cells and passed to its offspring, e.g. a knockout mouse or a goat producing human antithrombin in its milk.
questions.question: What is a transgenic animal?

questions.answer: Exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes; it occurs in the pachytene stage of prophase I of meiosis and gives genetic recombination.
questions.question: What is crossing over and when does it occur?

questions.answer:
1. Receptor = protein that binds a specific ligand and changes cell activity; agonists activate, antagonists block.
2. Families: ligand-gated ion channels (ms; nicotinic, GABA-A, NMDA); GPCRs (s; β-adrenergic, muscarinic, opioid); enzyme-linked (min–h; insulin and EGF receptor tyrosine kinases, TGF-β, cytokine/JAK, guanylyl cyclase); nuclear receptors (h–days; steroid, thyroid, vitamin D).
3. GPCR structure: single chain with seven transmembrane helices; G protein αβγ.
4. G protein cycle: GDP-bound inactive; receptor exchanges GDP for GTP; Gα-GTP and βγ act on effectors; GTPase switches off.
5. Gs → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA (R2C2; cAMP frees C) → phosphorylation of enzymes and CREB; PDE breaks cAMP (theophylline inhibits). Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase.
6. Gq → phospholipase C-β → PIP2 → IP3 (Ca2+ from ER) + DAG; DAG + Ca2+ → PKC; Ca2+–calmodulin kinases.
7. Examples: adrenaline on liver (glycogenolysis) and heart (β1); α1 on smooth muscle (Gq).
8. Termination and desensitisation: GTPase, PDE, phosphatases, GRK + β-arrestin, internalisation, down-regulation (tolerance).
9. Toxins: cholera (Gs locked on), pertussis (Gi locked off).
questions.question: Classify cell surface and intracellular receptors. Describe G protein-coupled receptors and the cAMP and phosphoinositide signalling pathways.

questions.answer:
1. Growth factor (EGF, PDGF) binds RTK → dimerisation → autophosphorylation of tyrosines.
2. Phosphotyrosines bind Grb2 (SH2) → SOS (exchange factor) → Ras-GDP to Ras-GTP.
3. Ras-GTP → Raf (MAPKKK) → MEK (MAPKK) → ERK (MAPK) → nucleus → transcription factors → proliferation.
4. Off: Ras GTPase with GAP; phosphatases; receptor internalisation.
5. Parallel PI3K–Akt pathway (PTEN opposes) and JAK–STAT for cytokines.
6. Misregulation: mutant Ras stuck GTP-bound (many cancers); BCR-ABL fusion in CML (imatinib); HER2 over-expression (trastuzumab, lapatinib); EGFR mutation in lung cancer (gefitinib, erlotinib); BRAF V600E melanoma (vemurafenib); PTEN loss; JAK2 V617F (ruxolitinib).
7. Non-cancer: cholera and pertussis toxins; insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes; autoantibodies (myasthenia gravis, Graves' disease); V2 receptor mutation (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus); NF-κB in inflammation.
8. Principle: gain-of-function of growth signals and loss of brakes cause cancer; drugs target the overactive step.
questions.question: Describe the receptor tyrosine kinase–Ras–MAP kinase pathway. Explain how misregulation of signalling pathways leads to disease, with drug examples.

questions.answer:
1. Protein kinases transfer the γ-phosphate of ATP to Ser, Thr or Tyr hydroxyl groups of proteins; phosphatases reverse it; about 500 human kinases.
2. Phosphorylation changes shape, activity, location or binding — a reversible switch.
3. Classes: Ser/Thr (PKA, PKC, PKG, CaMK, Akt, Raf, ERK, CDKs); receptor Tyr (insulin receptor, EGFR, HER2); non-receptor Tyr (Src, Abl, JAK, BTK); dual-specificity (MEK).
4. Structure: kinase domain of 250–300 amino acids; N-lobe (β-sheet, glycine-rich loop), C-lobe (α-helix, substrate binding); ATP cleft between lobes; activation loop.
5. Regulation: second messengers (cAMP–PKA, DAG/Ca2+–PKC, cGMP–PKG), partner proteins (cyclins, calmodulin), cascades (Raf → MEK → ERK), autophosphorylation, pseudosubstrate, inhibitor proteins (p21), scaffolds (AKAPs), phosphatases (calcineurin, inhibited by ciclosporin and tacrolimus).
6. Functions: metabolism, transcription, cell cycle, growth, contraction, memory, immunity.
7. Drugs (ATP-competitive, '-tinib'): imatinib, gefitinib, erlotinib, lapatinib, sorafenib, vemurafenib, trametinib, palbociclib, ibrutinib, tofacitinib, ruxolitinib; resistance by gatekeeper mutations (T315I).
questions.question: What are protein kinases? Describe their classification, structure, regulation and importance as drug targets.

questions.answer:
1. Endocrine: hormone through blood to distant targets (insulin, adrenaline, thyroxine).
2. Paracrine: local diffusion to nearby cells (growth factors, histamine, NO).
3. Autocrine: acts on the releasing cell (IL-2 on T cells, tumour growth factors).
4. Synaptic: neurotransmitter across a synapse (acetylcholine, noradrenaline).
5. Contact-dependent (juxtacrine): membrane-bound ligand and receptor touch (Notch–Delta, immune recognition).
6. Gap junctions: direct passage of small molecules (Ca2+, cAMP).
7. Signal molecules: hydrophilic → surface receptors; lipophilic → intracellular receptors; gases (NO) → enzymes.
questions.question: Explain the types of cell signalling based on distance with examples.

questions.answer:
1. Ligands are lipophilic: steroid hormones, thyroid hormones, vitamin D, retinoids.
2. They cross the membrane and bind receptors in cytoplasm (glucocorticoid receptor held by heat-shock proteins) or nucleus (thyroid receptor).
3. Receptor domains: ligand-binding, DNA-binding (zinc fingers), activation domain.
4. Hormone binding releases chaperones; complex dimerises and moves to the nucleus.
5. It binds hormone response elements in DNA, recruits co-activators and changes transcription.
6. New proteins are made, so onset is slow (hours) and effects last long; explains delayed action of corticosteroids.
questions.question: Describe the mechanism of action of intracellular (nuclear) receptors.

questions.answer:
1. Small intracellular molecules formed after receptor activation that carry and amplify the signal.
2. cAMP: made by adenylyl cyclase (Gs), activates PKA; broken by PDE.
3. cGMP: made by guanylyl cyclase (NO, ANP), activates PKG; PDE5 breaks it (sildenafil inhibits).
4. IP3: from PIP2 by PLC (Gq); releases Ca2+ from ER.
5. DAG: with Ca2+ activates PKC.
6. Ca2+: binds calmodulin, activates CaM kinases, myosin light-chain kinase, secretion.
7. PIP3: made by PI3K; recruits Akt.
8. Features: rapid formation and removal, amplification, diffusion within the cell.
questions.question: Write a note on second messengers.

questions.answer:
1. Desensitisation = reduced response on continued exposure to an agonist.
2. Homologous: GRK phosphorylates the active receptor; β-arrestin binds and uncouples it from the G protein.
3. Internalisation: β-arrestin promotes endocytosis of receptors; some recycle, some are degraded.
4. Heterologous: second-messenger kinases (PKA, PKC) phosphorylate receptors, affecting other receptors too.
5. Down-regulation: prolonged agonist reduces receptor number (tolerance to β2-agonists, nitrates); prolonged antagonist causes up-regulation (rebound on stopping β-blockers abruptly).
6. Importance in dosing and withdrawal.
questions.question: Explain receptor desensitisation and down-regulation.

questions.answer: It ADP-ribosylates the α subunit of Gs so it cannot hydrolyse GTP; adenylyl cyclase stays active, cAMP rises in intestinal cells and causes massive loss of Cl− and water.
questions.question: How does cholera toxin cause diarrhoea?

questions.answer: An enzyme that transfers the terminal phosphate of ATP to the hydroxyl group of serine, threonine or tyrosine in a protein, switching its activity; e.g. PKA, PKC, EGFR tyrosine kinase.
questions.question: What is a protein kinase?

units.markdown:
# Unit 1: Cells, membranes and the chemical foundations of life

This unit covers the first block of the syllabus: what cell and molecular biology is, its history, the properties of cells and the cell membrane, prokaryotic versus eukaryotic cells, how cells reproduce, and the chemistry that every cell is built on.

## 1.1 Definitions, basic theory and applications

**Cell biology** is the study of cells: their structure, the organelles inside them, how they interact with their surroundings, how they grow, divide and die.

**Molecular biology** is the study of life at the level of molecules, mainly DNA, RNA and proteins: how genetic information is stored, copied, read and controlled.

**Cell and molecular biology** joins the two. It explains what a cell does (cell biology) by the molecules that do it (molecular biology). For example, cell division is a cell event, but it is driven by cyclin proteins, kinases and the copying of DNA.

**The cell theory** (the basic theory of the subject):

1. All living organisms are made of one or more cells.
2. The cell is the basic unit of structure and function of life.
3. New cells arise only from cells that already exist.

Modern additions: cells carry hereditary information (DNA) that passes to daughter cells; all cells have broadly the same chemical make-up; energy flow (metabolism) happens inside cells.

**The central dogma** (the basic theory of molecular biology): genetic information flows DNA → RNA → protein. DNA copies itself (replication), DNA is copied into RNA (transcription) and RNA is read to make protein (translation). Exceptions: retroviruses copy RNA back into DNA (reverse transcription) and some viruses copy RNA from RNA.

**Applications in pharmacy and medicine**

| Area | How cell and molecular biology is used | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drug targets | Drugs act on receptors, enzymes, ion channels and transporters identified by molecular methods | Kinase inhibitors such as imatinib |
| Recombinant proteins | Human genes expressed in bacteria, yeast or animal cells | Human insulin, growth hormone, erythropoietin |
| Monoclonal antibodies | Hybridoma and recombinant cell technology | Trastuzumab, rituximab |
| Vaccines | Recombinant antigens and mRNA vaccines | Hepatitis B surface antigen vaccine |
| Diagnosis | Detecting genes and pathogens by PCR and probes | PCR test for infections, genetic screening |
| Gene therapy | Delivering a working gene into patient cells | Viral vectors for inherited disorders |
| Pharmacogenomics | Matching drug and dose to a patient's genes | CYP2C9 and VKORC1 variants and warfarin response |
| Toxicology and cancer | Understanding mutation, cell cycle loss of control, apoptosis | Anticancer drugs acting on dividing cells |

## 1.2 History of cell and molecular biology

| Year | Scientist | Contribution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1665 | Robert Hooke | Saw small compartments in cork with a simple microscope and called them "cells" |
| 1670s | Antonie van Leeuwenhoek | First saw living single cells (bacteria, protozoa, sperm) — "animalcules" |
| 1831 | Robert Brown | Described the nucleus in plant cells |
| 1838–1839 | Schleiden (plants) and Schwann (animals) | Proposed the cell theory |
| 1855 | Rudolf Virchow | "Omnis cellula e cellula" — every cell comes from a cell |
| 1866 | Gregor Mendel | Laws of inheritance from pea experiments |
| 1869 | Friedrich Miescher | Isolated "nuclein" (nucleic acid) from pus cells |
| 1928 | Frederick Griffith | Transformation of pneumococci — a "transforming principle" |
| 1944 | Avery, MacLeod and McCarty | Showed the transforming principle is DNA |
| 1950 | Erwin Chargaff | Base ratios: A = T and G = C |
| 1952 | Hershey and Chase | Phage experiment confirmed DNA as the genetic material |
| 1953 | Watson and Crick (using X-ray data of Franklin and Wilkins) | Double helix model of DNA |
| 1958 | Meselson and Stahl | Replication is semiconservative |
| 1958 | Francis Crick | Stated the central dogma |
| 1961 | Jacob and Monod | Operon model of gene regulation (lac operon) |
| 1961–1966 | Nirenberg, Khorana and others | Cracked the genetic code |
| 1970 | Temin and Baltimore | Reverse transcriptase |
| 1972 | Singer and Nicolson | Fluid mosaic model of the membrane |
| 1973 | Cohen and Boyer | First recombinant DNA in bacteria |
| 1977 | Frederick Sanger | Chain-termination DNA sequencing |
| 1983 | Kary Mullis | Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) |
| 2003 | Human Genome Project | Human genome sequence completed |

**Summation (the main lessons of the history):** the cell is the unit of life; heredity is carried by DNA; DNA is a double helix copied semiconservatively; genes are read through RNA into protein by a universal code; gene activity is regulated; and DNA can now be cut, joined, copied and read, which created biotechnology.

## 1.3 Properties of cells

All cells, from bacteria to human neurons, share these properties:

1. **Highly complex and organised** — molecules are arranged into organelles and structures in a fixed pattern.
2. **Carry a genetic program** — genes in DNA hold the instructions to build and run the cell.
3. **Reproduce** — one cell divides into two, passing a copy of the DNA to each.
4. **Acquire and use energy** — from light (plants) or food (animals); energy is stored as ATP.
5. **Carry out chemical reactions** — metabolism, speeded up by enzymes.
6. **Perform mechanical activities** — moving materials, contraction, beating of cilia and flagella, chromosome movement.
7. **Respond to stimuli** — through receptors on the surface or inside the cell.
8. **Self-regulate** — feedback keeps the internal state steady (homeostasis); damage is repaired.
9. **Evolve** — genes change over generations.

**Cell size.** Most bacteria are about 1–5 µm; most animal cells about 10–30 µm. Cells stay small because a small cell has a large surface area for its volume, which allows fast exchange of nutrients and wastes.

## 1.4 The cell membrane (plasma membrane)

The plasma membrane is the thin boundary (about 7–10 nm thick) that separates the cell from its surroundings and controls what enters and leaves.

### Fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972)

The membrane is a **fluid lipid bilayer** in which **proteins float like icebergs in a sea of lipid**. "Fluid" because lipids and many proteins move sideways; "mosaic" because many different proteins are scattered in it.

```text
        Outside the cell (extracellular fluid)
     glycoprotein      glycolipid
         |  sugar chains  |
   ooooooo|oooooooooooooooo|ooooooo   <- polar heads (hydrophilic)
   ||||||[==== integral ====]||||||   <- fatty acid tails (hydrophobic core)
   ||||||[==== protein  ====]||||||
   ooooooooooooooo[peripheral]ooooo   <- polar heads
                   protein
        Inside the cell (cytoplasm)
```

### Membrane components

| Component | Description | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Phospholipids | Phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylserine, sphingomyelin; amphipathic (polar head + two fatty acid tails) | Form the bilayer; barrier to polar molecules |
| Cholesterol | Sits between phospholipids in animal membranes | Controls fluidity — stiffens at high temperature, keeps fluid at low temperature |
| Glycolipids | Lipids with sugar chains, outer face only | Cell recognition, blood group antigens |
| Integral (intrinsic) proteins | Pass through the bilayer (transmembrane) | Channels, carriers, receptors |
| Peripheral (extrinsic) proteins | Attached to the surface or to integral proteins | Enzymes, links to cytoskeleton |
| Lipid-anchored proteins | Held by a covalently attached lipid | Signalling proteins such as Ras |
| Carbohydrates | Attached to proteins and lipids on the outer face — the glycocalyx | Recognition, adhesion, protection |

**Membrane asymmetry:** the two layers differ. Phosphatidylserine faces the inside; its appearance on the outside is a signal of apoptosis. Sugar chains face only outward.

**Membrane fluidity** rises with shorter and unsaturated (kinked) fatty acid chains and with higher temperature; cholesterol buffers the change.

### Functions of the plasma membrane

1. Boundary and selective permeability barrier.
2. Transport of solutes and ions.
3. Receiving signals (receptors) and passing them inside.
4. Cell-to-cell recognition and adhesion (junctions).
5. Holding enzymes and anchoring the cytoskeleton.
6. Keeping ion gradients and the membrane potential.

### Transport across the membrane

| Type | Energy | Carrier | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Simple diffusion | None (down gradient) | No | O2, CO2, small lipid-soluble drugs |
| Facilitated diffusion — channel | None | Channel protein | K+ channels, aquaporins for water |
| Facilitated diffusion — carrier | None | Carrier, shows saturation | GLUT glucose transporters |
| Primary active transport | ATP directly | Pump | Na+/K+-ATPase (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in per ATP) |
| Secondary active transport | Ion gradient made by a pump | Symporter or antiporter | Na+–glucose symport (SGLT) in gut and kidney; Na+/Ca2+ exchanger |
| Endocytosis | ATP | Vesicles | Phagocytosis, pinocytosis, receptor-mediated uptake of LDL |
| Exocytosis | ATP | Vesicles | Release of hormones and neurotransmitters |

Most drugs cross membranes by passive diffusion of the un-ionised form; some use carriers (levodopa uses an amino acid carrier) or are pumped out by efflux pumps such as P-glycoprotein, which causes drug resistance in cancer cells.

## 1.5 Prokaryotic versus eukaryotic cells

| Feature | Prokaryotic cell | Eukaryotic cell |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Examples | Bacteria, archaea | Protozoa, fungi, plants, animals |
| Size | Usually 1–10 µm | Usually 10–100 µm |
| Nucleus | No true nucleus; DNA in a nucleoid region | True nucleus with a double nuclear envelope |
| DNA | Usually one circular chromosome; plasmids common; few or no histones | Several linear chromosomes wound on histones (chromatin) |
| Membrane-bound organelles | Absent | Present: mitochondria, ER, Golgi, lysosomes, chloroplasts in plants |
| Ribosomes | 70S (50S + 30S) | 80S in cytoplasm (60S + 40S); 70S in mitochondria and chloroplasts |
| Cell wall | Usually present; peptidoglycan in bacteria | Absent in animals; cellulose in plants, chitin in fungi |
| Cytoskeleton | Simple protein homologues | Well developed: microfilaments, microtubules, intermediate filaments |
| Cell division | Binary fission | Mitosis and meiosis |
| Gene structure | Introns rare; genes often in operons | Introns common; one gene per mRNA usually |
| Transcription and translation | Coupled — both in cytoplasm at the same time | Separated — transcription in nucleus, translation in cytoplasm |
| Flagella | Simple, made of flagellin, rotate | Complex 9 + 2 microtubule structure, whip-like |

**Pharmaceutical importance:** antibiotics act on features found only in prokaryotes — peptidoglycan cell wall (penicillins), 70S ribosomes (tetracyclines act on 30S, macrolides and chloramphenicol on 50S), bacterial DNA gyrase (fluoroquinolones). This selective toxicity is possible because of the differences in the table.

### Main eukaryotic organelles

| Organelle | Structure | Function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nucleus | Double envelope with nuclear pores; nucleolus inside | Stores DNA; site of replication and transcription; nucleolus makes rRNA and ribosome subunits |
| Rough ER | Membranes studded with ribosomes | Synthesis of secretory and membrane proteins |
| Smooth ER | No ribosomes | Lipid synthesis, drug detoxification (cytochrome P450 in liver), Ca2+ storage |
| Golgi apparatus | Stacked flattened sacs (cis and trans faces) | Modifies (glycosylation), sorts and packs proteins into vesicles |
| Lysosomes | Membrane sacs with acid hydrolases (pH about 5) | Digestion of worn-out parts and engulfed material |
| Mitochondria | Double membrane; inner folded into cristae; own DNA and 70S-type ribosomes | ATP by oxidative phosphorylation; also controls apoptosis |
| Peroxisomes | Single membrane, contain catalase and oxidases | Break down fatty acids and hydrogen peroxide |
| Ribosomes | rRNA + protein, free or on ER | Protein synthesis |
| Cytoskeleton | Microfilaments (actin, about 7 nm), intermediate filaments (about 10 nm), microtubules (tubulin, about 25 nm) | Shape, movement, transport, chromosome separation |
| Centrosome | Two centrioles (animal cells) | Organises microtubules and the mitotic spindle |

## 1.6 Cellular reproduction

Cells multiply by dividing. Before dividing, the cell copies its DNA and then shares it equally.

**In prokaryotes — binary fission:**

1. The circular chromosome is copied from a single origin.
2. The two copies attach to the membrane and move apart as the cell grows.
3. A septum forms in the middle and the cell splits into two identical cells.

Under good conditions *E. coli* can divide about every 20 minutes.

**In eukaryotes — the cell cycle:**

```text
   G1 (growth) → S (DNA synthesis) → G2 (preparation) → M (mitosis + cytokinesis)
     ^                                                         |
     |_________________________________________________________|
   Cells that stop dividing leave G1 and enter G0 (resting)
```

- **Mitosis** gives two daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent (diploid → diploid). It is used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.
- **Meiosis** gives four cells with half the chromosome number (diploid → haploid gametes) and shuffles genes. It is used for sexual reproduction.

The phases and checkpoints of the cycle are covered in detail in Unit 4.

## 1.7 Chemical foundations of the cell

### Elements and water

About 99% of the mass of a cell is made of hydrogen, oxygen, carbon and nitrogen; phosphorus and sulphur are also important. **Water** makes up about 70% of cell mass. Water is polar, forms hydrogen bonds, dissolves ions and polar molecules, has a high specific heat (keeps temperature steady) and drives the **hydrophobic effect** — non-polar groups cluster together to avoid water, which is why membranes form and proteins fold.

### Chemical bonds in the cell

| Bond | Strength | Where it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Covalent | Strong (sharing of electrons) | Backbone of all biomolecules; peptide and phosphodiester bonds |
| Ionic | Weak in water | Salt bridges between charged amino acids |
| Hydrogen bond | Weak | DNA base pairing, protein secondary structure |
| Van der Waals forces | Very weak, short range | Close packing inside proteins; drug–receptor fit |
| Hydrophobic interactions | Weak, entropy-driven | Lipid bilayer, protein folding |

Many weak bonds together make a structure stable but easy to change, which is exactly what living molecules need (DNA strands can be separated; drugs bind and leave receptors).

### The four classes of biomolecules

| Class | Building block (monomer) | Linking bond | Main roles |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Carbohydrates | Monosaccharides (glucose) | Glycosidic bond | Energy (glucose, glycogen), structure (cellulose), recognition |
| Lipids | Fatty acids and glycerol (not true polymers) | Ester bond | Membranes, energy store, hormones (steroids) |
| Proteins | 20 amino acids | Peptide bond | Enzymes, structure, transport, receptors, antibodies |
| Nucleic acids | Nucleotides | Phosphodiester bond | Store and transfer genetic information |

Large molecules are built by **condensation (dehydration) reactions**, which remove water, and broken down by **hydrolysis**, which adds water.

### Types of biochemical reactions

1. **Oxidation–reduction (redox)** — transfer of electrons, often with hydrogen; carriers NAD+/NADH and FAD/FADH2. Example: oxidation of glucose to CO2.
2. **Group transfer** — moving a chemical group from one molecule to another, e.g. phosphate transfer from ATP by kinases.
3. **Hydrolysis** — breaking a bond with water, e.g. digestion of proteins by proteases.
4. **Condensation** — joining molecules with release of water, e.g. peptide bond formation.
5. **Isomerisation (rearrangement)** — atoms rearranged in the same molecule, e.g. glucose 6-phosphate ⇌ fructose 6-phosphate.
6. **Making or breaking carbon–carbon bonds** — e.g. aldolase cleavage in glycolysis.
7. **Elimination and addition** — removing or adding groups across a double bond, e.g. water removal by dehydratases.

### Energy, ATP and enzymes

- **Free energy change (ΔG)** tells whether a reaction can occur on its own. ΔG negative = **exergonic** (spontaneous, releases energy); ΔG positive = **endergonic** (needs energy input).
- Cells drive endergonic reactions by **coupling** them to ATP hydrolysis: ATP + H2O → ADP + Pi, ΔG°′ about −30.5 kJ/mol (−7.3 kcal/mol).
- **Enzymes** are biological catalysts, mostly proteins (some are RNA — ribozymes). They lower the **activation energy**, speed reactions many-fold, are specific for their substrate and are not used up. They do not change ΔG or the equilibrium position.
- **Michaelis–Menten equation:** v = Vmax [S] / (Km + [S]). Km is the substrate concentration giving half Vmax; a low Km means high affinity.
- Many drugs are enzyme inhibitors: competitive inhibitors raise Km (Vmax unchanged); non-competitive inhibitors lower Vmax (Km unchanged).

## Remember

- Cell theory: all organisms are cells; the cell is the unit of life; cells come only from cells (Virchow).
- Central dogma: DNA → RNA → protein; reverse transcriptase is the main exception.
- Watson and Crick 1953 (double helix); Meselson–Stahl 1958 (semiconservative); Jacob–Monod 1961 (operon); Singer–Nicolson 1972 (fluid mosaic); Mullis 1983 (PCR).
- Membrane = fluid lipid bilayer + proteins + cholesterol + glycocalyx; about 7–10 nm thick.
- Na+/K+-ATPase moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP.
- Prokaryotes: no nucleus, 70S ribosomes, circular DNA, peptidoglycan wall, binary fission. Eukaryotes: nucleus, 80S ribosomes, linear chromosomes on histones, organelles.
- Weak bonds (hydrogen, ionic, van der Waals, hydrophobic) shape biomolecules; covalent bonds form their backbones.
- ΔG negative = exergonic; enzymes lower activation energy but not ΔG.
